lead: A force is not just a push of some size; it also points somewhere. Mechanics therefore treats force as a vector: a quantity with magnitude and direction that adds by geometry, not by simple arithmetic. Two 3 N pulls at right angles give about 4.24 N, not 6 N. This chapter sets up vector notation, addition and subtraction, the dot and cross products, and i, j, k components. These tools turn concurrent-force problems into short component sums and prepare the equilibrium work in the next chapters.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for force as a quantity, units and the particle model.

blocks.text: A scalar has size only: mass 5 kg, time 12 s, temperature 40 °C, work 60 J. A vector has size and direction: displacement 30 m north, velocity 12 m/s east, force 20 N along a rope. Force is a vector because its effect changes when its direction changes.
Write a vector as A (bold) or with an arrow. Its size is A or |A|, a positive scalar in the same unit. A unit vector has size 1 and keeps direction.

blocks.where: Â is the unit vector along A; A is the magnitude of A; Â has no unit.

blocks.text: The position vector r of a point P is the arrow from the origin O to P. It fixes where P is relative to O.
r = x i + y j + z k
blocks.where: r is the position vector in metres; x, y, z are the coordinates of P in metres; i, j, k are unit vectors along the x, y, z axes.

blocks.text: Two vectors are equal when their magnitudes and directions match. In particle mechanics all forces act at one point, so two forces with the same magnitude and direction are equivalent even if drawn at different places on the page. For a rigid body the line of action matters; see Unit 2.
The triangle law adds two vectors. Place the tail of B at the head of A; the resultant R runs from the tail of A to the head of B.

items: Draw A to scale with an arrow.
From the head of A, draw B to scale.
Draw R = A + B from the start of A to the end of B.
Read the length of R for magnitude and its angle for direction.

blocks.text: The parallelogram law gives the same result. Draw A and B from one point, complete the parallelogram, and take the diagonal from that point as A + B. This is why two forces at a point are combined by the diagonal, not by adding their sizes.

Subtraction is addition of the negative: A − B = A + (−B). The vector −B has the same size as B and the opposite direction. Multiplying by a scalar c changes the size to |c|B; if c is negative, the direction reverses.
Sizes add only when the vectors are parallel and in the same direction. At any other angle, use the triangle or parallelogram construction, or add components.

sections.h3: Components, dot product and cross product

blocks.text: In three dimensions a vector is fixed by three components along i, j, k.
A = Ax i + Ay j + Az k
blocks.where: Ax, Ay, Az are the components in the same unit as A; i, j, k are unit vectors along x, y, z.
A is the magnitude of A, in the same unit as its components.

blocks.text: The dot product multiplies two vectors to give a scalar. The angle θ is measured between the two vectors placed tail to tail.

blocks.where: A·B is a scalar; A and B are the magnitudes; θ is the angle between them, in degrees or radians.

blocks.text: The cross product gives a vector perpendicular to both. Its direction follows the right-hand rule: curl the fingers from A to B, and the thumb points along A × B.

blocks.where: |A × B| is the magnitude of the cross product; θ is the smaller angle between the vectors, 0° to 180°.

blocks.text: For vectors in the xy plane, A × B = (AxBy − AyBx) k. A positive result points along +k, out of the page. The angle between two vectors follows from cos θ = A·B/(AB).
Component addition, resolution and resultants of several forces are worked out in Chapter 1.3 and Chapter 1.4.

figure.caption: Vector algebra splits into addition, the scalar dot product and the vector cross product. Notice that subtraction is just addition of the reversed vector.

spec.aria: A tree puts vector algebra into three branches: addition with the triangle, parallelogram and subtraction rules, the scalar dot product, and the vector cross product.

examples.question: Forces F1 = 3i + 4j N and F2 = 4i + 3j N act at a particle. Find F1 + F2, F1 − F2, F1·F2, F1 × F2, and the angle between the two forces.
steps: Magnitude = √(7² + 7²) = 7√2 = 9.90 N. Direction = tan<sup>−1</sup>(7/7) = 45° from the +x axis.
Magnitude = √((−1)² + 1²) = √2 = 1.41 N. Direction = 135° from the +x axis.
Cross product in the plane: F1 × F2 = (3 × 3 − 4 × 4)k = −7k N². Its magnitude is 7 N² and it points into the page. Check: 5 × 5 × sin 16.26° = 7.00 N².
examples.answer: F1 + F2 = 7i + 7j N (9.90 N at 45°); F1 − F2 = −i + j N (1.41 N at 135°); F1·F2 = 24 N²; F1 × F2 = −7k N²; the angle is 16.26°.
examples.check:
import math
ax, ay = 3.0, 4.0
bx, by = 4.0, 3.0
sx, sy = ax + bx, ay + by
print(f'{math.hypot(sx, sy):.2f}')
print(f'{math.degrees(math.atan2(sy, sx)):.2f}')
dx, dy = ax - bx, ay - by
print(f'{math.hypot(dx, dy):.2f}')
print(f'{math.degrees(math.atan2(dy, dx)):.2f}')
print(f'{ax*bx + ay*by:.2f}')
m1 = math.hypot(ax, ay)
m2 = math.hypot(bx, by)
c = (ax*bx + ay*by)/(m1*m2)
print(f'{math.degrees(math.acos(c)):.2f}')
cz = ax*by - ay*bx
print(f'{cz:.2f}')
print(f'{abs(cz):.2f}')

traps: Adding magnitudes as if vectors were scalars: 3 N + 4 N is 7 N only when the forces are parallel and in the same direction.
Writing a vector answer as a bare number, such as 9.90 N, with no direction. A vector answer needs magnitude and direction, or components.
Using the dot-product angle as a bearing. cos θ = A·B/(AB) gives the angle between the vectors, 0° to 180°, not the angle from the x-axis.
Reversing a cross product: A × B = −(B × A). The sign decides whether the vector points out of or into the page.
Mixing units or calculator modes. Components must share one unit before adding, and θ must match the degree or radian setting.

quiz.q: Define a scalar and a vector, and give one mechanics example of each.
quiz.a: A scalar has magnitude only, such as mass 5 kg. A vector has magnitude and direction, such as force 20 N along a rope.

quiz.q: Why is 3 N + 4 N not always 7 N?
quiz.a: Forces add by the triangle law. The magnitude of the sum depends on the angle. Sizes add only when the forces are parallel and in the same direction; at 90° the sum is 5 N.

quiz.q: A = 2i + 3j N and B = 4i − j N. Find A·B and the angle between them.

quiz.a: For plane vectors, A × B = (AxBy − AyBx)k = (2 × −2 − 3 × 1)k = −7k. Magnitude 7, direction into the page.

quiz.q: For two nonzero vectors, what does A·B = 0 tell you? What does A × B = 0 tell you?
quiz.a: A·B = 0 means cos θ = 0, so the vectors are perpendicular. A × B = 0 means sin θ = 0, so the vectors are parallel or antiparallel.

quiz.q: Two forces of equal magnitude F act at a point. Show that |F1 + F2| = |F1 − F2| when the forces are perpendicular.
quiz.a: |F1 + F2|² = 2F² + 2F1·F2. |F1 − F2|² = 2F² − 2F1·F2. They are equal when F1·F2 = 0, which is the perpendicular condition.

quiz.q: Write the unit vector along a vector A.
quiz.a: Â = A/A, where A is the magnitude of A.

beyond: Not for the exam. Vector algebra is the language of computer graphics, robotics, GPS and structural software. Game engines use dot products for lighting and cross products for surface normals. Finite element packages assemble force vectors with the same rules. Search next: vector dot product in shading, cross product in robot kinematics, and direction cosines.
